set_title: Neck flexion and nerve-root signs: Kernig sign, Brudzinski sign, Lhermitte sign, Lasegue sign (straight leg raise) and Spurling sign
stem: A 34-year-old warehouse worker has low back pain after lifting a heavy crate. Raising his extended right leg to 40 degrees shoots pain down the posterior thigh below the knee. He is afebrile, his neck is supple, and his right ankle reflex is diminished.
oneliner: 34M, back pain after lifting + straight leg raise shoots pain below knee → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

options.B: Cervical cord demyelination in multiple sclerosis
options.D: Femoral nerve entrapment at the inguinal ligament
options.E: Lumbar disc herniation compressing a root

whyNot.A: Meningitis causes fever and neck stiffness; he is **afebrile with a supple neck**
whyNot.B: Demyelination gives upper motor neuron signs; his **ankle reflex is diminished**
whyNot.C: Cervical root disease causes arm symptoms; his pain is in the **posterior leg**
whyNot.D: Femoral entrapment gives anterior thigh pain; his pain is **posterior, below the knee**

answer: Lumbar disc herniation compressing a root
why: Pain shooting below the knee on **straight leg raise** is the Lasegue sign. Here it indicates L5 or S1 root compression by a herniated lumbar disc.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Knee extension with hip flexed is painful
Neck flexion makes hips and knees flex
Neck flexion sends electric shock down spine
Cervical cord demyelination, e.g. multiple sclerosis
Raising straight leg shoots pain below knee
L5 or S1 radiculopathy from disc herniation
Neck extension, rotation, compression reproduces arm pain

idea.rule: Pain below knee on straight leg raise = L5 or S1 root compression.
also: Positive between 30 and 70 degrees
Crossed sign is more specific

set_title: Muscle and calcium signs: Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign of hypocalcemia, Gowers sign, Grip myotonia and Post-exercise facilitation
stem: A 4-year-old boy has frequent falls and trouble climbing stairs. His calves look enlarged. To rise from the floor he turns prone, then pushes his hands up along his thighs to straighten his trunk. Creatine kinase is 18,000 U/L.
oneliner: 4-year-old boy, falls, big calves, CK 18,000 + pushes hands up thighs to stand → ?

whyNot.B: Chvostek is a facial twitch on tapping; his finding is **hands climbing the thighs**
whyNot.C: Trousseau is carpal spasm from a cuff; his finding is **hands climbing the thighs**
whyNot.D: Grip myotonia is slow hand release; his difficulty is **rising from the floor**
whyNot.E: Facilitation is strength improving with effort; his weakness is **proximal with CK 18,000**

why: Climbing the hands up the legs to stand compensates for weak pelvic girdle muscles. Big calves and **CK 18,000** point to Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

idea.rule: Hands climbing up the thighs to rise = Gowers, proximal weakness, think Duchenne.
also: X-linked dystrophin mutation
Calf pseudohypertrophy

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Tapping facial nerve twitches the face
BP cuff inflation causes carpal spasm
Climbs hands up legs to stand
Strength and reflexes improve with effort

set_title: Nail signs: Clubbing, Koilonychia, Beau lines, Mees lines, Nail pitting and Terry nails
stem: A 45-year-old man has had 6 months of swelling and pain in the distal interphalangeal joints of both hands, with morning stiffness lasting 1 hour. Multiple small, punched-out pits are present in his fingernails. He has had no recent infection.
oneliner: 45M, distal interphalangeal joint arthritis + punctate nail pits → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: Osteoarthritis spares nails and has brief stiffness; he has **nail pits and 1-hour stiffness**
whyNot.C: Rheumatoid arthritis spares the distal joints; he has **DIP arthritis and nail pits**
whyNot.D: Gout gives acute monoarticular attacks; his is **chronic DIP swelling with nail pits**
whyNot.E: Reactive arthritis follows infection; he has **no recent infection** and has nail pits

why: Punched-out nail pits mark psoriatic nail disease, which predicts psoriatic arthritis. **Distal joint arthritis with nail pits** fits.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Loss of nail fold angle, bulbous tips
Nail growth arrest: chemotherapy, severe illness
Small punched-out pits in nail plate
White nail with thin distal red band

idea.rule: Nail pits + DIP arthritis = psoriatic arthritis.
also: Pencil-in-cup deformity on x-ray
Dactylitis and HLA-B27 are associated

set_title: Hand joint deformities: Heberden nodes, Bouchard nodes, Swan neck deformity, Boutonniere deformity, Sausage digit and Tophi
stem: A 68-year-old woman has had 10 years of hand pain that worsens through the day and improves with rest. Morning stiffness lasts 10 minutes. Examination shows hard, bony swellings at the distal interphalangeal joints of several fingers, without warmth.
oneliner: 68F, evening hand pain + bony swellings of distal finger joints → ?

whyNot.B: Bouchard nodes affect the proximal joints; hers are at **the distal interphalangeal joints**
whyNot.C: Swan neck is PIP hyperextension; she has **bony DIP swellings**
whyNot.D: Boutonniere is PIP flexion; she has **bony DIP swellings**
whyNot.E: Tophi are chalky nodules of gout; hers are **hard, bony, nontender DIP swellings**

why: Bony swelling at the distal interphalangeal joints is Heberden nodes, a marker of osteoarthritis. **Pain worse by evening and brief morning stiffness** support degeneration.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Whole finger or toe diffusely swollen
Chalky nodules on ears, joints, tendons

idea.rule: Bony DIP nodes + pain worse with use = Heberden nodes = osteoarthritis.
also: Bouchard nodes are the PIP equivalent
MCP joints are spared

set_title: Hand joint deformities: Heberden nodes, Bouchard nodes, Swan neck deformity, Boutonniere deformity, Sausage digit and Tophi
stem: A 53-year-old woman has had 6 years of symmetric hand pain with morning stiffness lasting over 1 hour. Her fingers show hyperextension at the proximal interphalangeal joints and flexion at the distal interphalangeal joints, with ulnar deviation at the metacarpophalangeal joints.
oneliner: 53F, symmetric hand stiffness + PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion → ?

whyNot.A: Heberden nodes are bony DIP swellings; she has **PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion**
whyNot.B: Boutonniere is PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension; hers is **the opposite pattern**
whyNot.C: Sausage digit is diffuse digit swelling; hers is **PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion**
whyNot.E: Tophi are chalky nodules in gout; she has **symmetric stiffness with finger deformity**

why: PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion is a swan neck deformity, a late change of rheumatoid arthritis. **Symmetric hand involvement with prolonged morning stiffness** fits.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Whole finger or toe diffusely swollen
Chalky nodules on ears, joints, tendons

idea.rule: PIP hyperextension + DIP flexion = swan neck = rheumatoid arthritis.
also: Boutonniere is the opposite, from central slip injury
Anti-CCP is most specific

set_title: Hand joint deformities: Heberden nodes, Bouchard nodes, Swan neck deformity, Boutonniere deformity, Sausage digit and Tophi
stem: A 42-year-old man has had 3 months of painless swelling of his entire second toe, which looks like a sausage. His fingernails have multiple small pits, and he has low back stiffness.
oneliner: 42M, whole second toe swollen + nail pits → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: Gout gives an acutely painful red joint; his swelling is **chronic with nail pits**
whyNot.B: Osteoarthritis causes bony nodes, not **whole-toe swelling with nail pits**
whyNot.D: RA causes symmetric synovitis and spares nails; he has **nail pits and dactylitis**
whyNot.E: Septic arthritis is one hot painful joint; his toe is **painless with nail pits**

why: Diffuse swelling of a whole digit (dactylitis) reflects flexor tenosynovitis plus joint inflammation, typical of psoriatic arthritis. **Nail pits** point to psoriasis.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Whole finger or toe diffusely swollen
Chalky nodules on ears, joints, tendons

idea.rule: Whole-digit swelling + nail pits = dactylitis = psoriatic arthritis.
also: Reactive arthritis also causes dactylitis
HLA-B27 is associated

set_title: Hand joint deformities: Heberden nodes, Bouchard nodes, Swan neck deformity, Boutonniere deformity, Sausage digit and Tophi
stem: A 58-year-old man with 12 years of recurrent episodes of acute toe pain has firm, chalky white nodules on the helix of both ears and over his elbow bursae (tophi). Aspiration of one nodule yields a chalky white paste.
oneliner: 58M, recurrent toe attacks + chalky nodules on ear helix → crystal?
ask: Which crystal is deposited in these nodules?

whyNot.B: CPPD causes pseudogout with knee chondrocalcinosis, not **chalky nodules on the ears**
whyNot.C: Calcium oxalate forms kidney stones, not **chalky joint and ear nodules**
whyNot.D: Hydroxyapatite causes calcific tendinitis, not **ear nodules after toe attacks**
whyNot.E: Cholesterol forms soft yellow xanthomas; his nodules are **chalky white after toe attacks**

why: Chalky nodules on the ears, joints and tendons are tophi: deposits of monosodium urate from chronic gout. **Recurrent toe attacks** reflect long-standing hyperuricemia.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Whole finger or toe diffusely swollen
Chalky nodules on ears, joints, tendons

idea.rule: Chalky ear or joint nodules = tophi = urate crystals of chronic gout.
also: Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals
Treat with allopurinol or febuxostat

set_title: Knee exam tests: McMurray test, Lachman test, Anterior drawer test, Posterior drawer test and Valgus stress test
stem: A 21-year-old soccer player heard a pop after planting his foot and pivoting, and the knee swelled within 2 hours. With the knee flexed about 20 degrees and the femur stabilized, the examiner pulls the tibia forward; it translates excessively with a soft endpoint.
oneliner: 21M soccer player, pop + swelling, forward tibial slide at 20 degrees → ?

whyNot.A: McMurray tests meniscus by rotation; this test **pulls the tibia forward at 20 degrees**
whyNot.B: Anterior drawer is done at 90 degrees; this test used **20 degrees of flexion**
whyNot.C: Posterior drawer pushes the tibia backward; here the tibia **translates forward**
whyNot.E: Valgus stress tests the MCL; here **the tibia pulls forward**

why: Excess anterior tibial translation with the knee near 20 degrees is a positive Lachman test, the most sensitive for ACL tear. **Pop after pivoting with rapid swelling** fits.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Painful click on rotating flexed knee
Tibia slides forward at 20-30 degrees flexion
Tibia pulls forward at 90 degrees flexion
Tibia pushes backward at 90 degrees flexion
Knee gaps medially under valgus force

idea.rule: Forward tibial slide at 20 degrees flexion = Lachman test = ACL tear.
also: More sensitive than anterior drawer
Unhappy triad: ACL, MCL, medial meniscus

set_title: Knee exam tests: McMurray test, Lachman test, Anterior drawer test, Posterior drawer test and Valgus stress test
stem: A 34-year-old man has had medial knee pain and episodes of locking since twisting his knee during a basketball game. With the knee fully flexed, the examiner rotates the tibia and extends the knee, producing a painful click along the medial joint line.
oneliner: 34M, locking knee + painful click on rotating flexed knee → ?

whyNot.A: Lachman measures forward tibial translation; this test **rotates the flexed knee with a click**
whyNot.C: Anterior drawer pulls the tibia forward; this test **rotates the flexed knee**
whyNot.D: Posterior drawer pushes the tibia backward; this test produces **a painful click on rotation**
whyNot.E: Valgus stress opens the medial joint; this test produces **a click with rotation**

why: A painful click when the flexed knee is rotated and extended is a positive McMurray test, indicating meniscal tear. **Locking and joint-line pain** support it.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Painful click on rotating flexed knee
Tibia slides forward at 20-30 degrees flexion
Tibia pulls forward at 90 degrees flexion
Tibia pushes backward at 90 degrees flexion
Knee gaps medially under valgus force

idea.rule: Click on rotating flexed knee + locking = McMurray test = meniscal tear.
also: Medial meniscus tears more often than lateral
MRI confirms the tear

set_title: Knee exam tests: McMurray test, Lachman test, Anterior drawer test, Posterior drawer test and Valgus stress test
stem: A 25-year-old man in a motor vehicle collision strikes his flexed knee against the dashboard. The knee is swollen and painful. With the knee at 90 degrees of flexion, the tibia sags backward when pushed (positive drawer test).
oneliner: 25M, dashboard injury + tibial sag backward at 90 degrees → ligament?

whyNot.A: ACL tear shows forward tibial translation; here the tibia **sags backward**
whyNot.B: MCL tear shows medial gapping on valgus stress; here the tibia **sags backward**
whyNot.C: LCL tear shows lateral gapping on varus stress; here the tibia **sags backward**
whyNot.D: MPFL injury causes patellar dislocation; here **the tibia sags backward at 90 degrees**

why: Posterior tibial sag at 90 degrees is a positive posterior drawer test. The PCL prevents posterior tibial translation, and a **dashboard injury** drives the flexed tibia backward.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Painful click on rotating flexed knee
Tibia slides forward at 20-30 degrees flexion
Tibia pulls forward at 90 degrees flexion
Tibia pushes backward at 90 degrees flexion
Knee gaps medially under valgus force

idea.rule: Posterior tibial sag at 90 degrees after dashboard injury = PCL tear.
also: Dashboard injury hits the proximal tibia
Falls on a flexed knee also injure it

set_title: Knee exam tests: McMurray test, Lachman test, Anterior drawer test, Posterior drawer test and Valgus stress test
stem: A 19-year-old football player is tackled by a blow to the outside of the right knee. Pain is localized to the inner side of the knee. With the knee flexed 30 degrees, a valgus force opens the inner joint space excessively.
oneliner: 19M football player, lateral knee blow + inner joint gapping on valgus force → ligament?

whyNot.A: LCL tear opens laterally on varus stress; here **the medial joint opens**
whyNot.B: ACL tear shows forward tibial translation; here **the medial joint opens on valgus force**
whyNot.C: PCL tear shows posterior tibial sag; here **the medial joint opens on valgus force**
whyNot.E: MPFL injury causes patellar instability; here **valgus force opens the medial joint**

why: Excess medial joint opening under valgus force at 30 degrees is a positive valgus stress test, indicating MCL tear. A **lateral blow to the knee** stresses the medial side.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Painful click on rotating flexed knee
Tibia slides forward at 20-30 degrees flexion
Tibia pulls forward at 90 degrees flexion
Tibia pushes backward at 90 degrees flexion
Knee gaps medially under valgus force

idea.rule: Lateral knee blow + medial gapping on valgus stress = MCL tear.
also: MCL tear is part of the unhappy triad
Medial meniscus attaches to the MCL

set_title: Shoulder exam tests: Drop arm test, Empty can test, Hawkins test, Apprehension test and Speed test
stem: A 64-year-old man fell on his outstretched arm 2 weeks ago and now cannot lift his right arm well. The examiner passively abducts the arm to 90 degrees; when he is asked to lower it slowly, the arm falls suddenly to his side.
oneliner: 64M, fall + arm suddenly drops when lowered from 90 degrees → ?

whyNot.A: Empty can resists downward force with thumb down; here **the arm drops when lowered**
whyNot.C: Hawkins elicits pain on internal rotation; he has **sudden arm drop**
whyNot.D: Apprehension test shows fear of dislocation; he has **sudden arm drop from 90 degrees**
whyNot.E: Speed test causes bicipital groove pain on resisted flexion; he has **arm drop**

why: An arm that falls when lowered from 90 degrees of abduction is a positive drop arm test, indicating a large supraspinatus (rotator cuff) tear. **The arm cannot be lowered slowly.**

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Arm falls when lowered from 90 degrees
Weak painful elevation with thumbs down
Pain on internal rotation of flexed arm
Fear when arm abducted, externally rotated
Pain on resisted forward flexion, palm up

idea.rule: Arm drops from 90 degrees abduction = drop arm test = supraspinatus tear.
also: Supraspinatus starts the first 15 degrees of abduction
Suprascapular nerve supplies it

set_title: Shoulder exam tests: Drop arm test, Empty can test, Hawkins test, Apprehension test and Speed test
stem: A 45-year-old house painter has had 2 months of right shoulder pain when working overhead. With both arms abducted to 90 degrees, flexed forward 30 degrees and thumbs pointing down, he has pain and weakness resisting downward pressure on the right arm. He can hold the position without dropping it.
oneliner: 45M painter, overhead pain + weak thumbs-down arm elevation → ?

whyNot.A: Drop arm is an arm that falls; he **holds position with pain and weakness**
whyNot.B: Hawkins is pain on internal rotation; his pain is **thumbs-down resisted elevation**
whyNot.C: Apprehension test is fear of dislocation; he has **pain and weakness with thumbs down**
whyNot.D: Speed test is palm-up resisted flexion with groove pain; he has **thumbs-down resisted elevation**

why: Pain and weakness on resisted elevation with thumbs pointing down is a positive empty can test, indicating supraspinatus tendinopathy or tear. **Overhead work** is the usual setting.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Arm falls when lowered from 90 degrees
Weak painful elevation with thumbs down
Pain on internal rotation of flexed arm
Fear when arm abducted, externally rotated
Pain on resisted forward flexion, palm up

idea.rule: Pain or weakness elevating thumb-down arm = empty can test = supraspinatus tendinopathy.
also: Most commonly injured rotator cuff muscle
Full can test is less painful

set_title: Shoulder exam tests: Drop arm test, Empty can test, Hawkins test, Apprehension test and Speed test
stem: A 38-year-old swimmer has had 3 months of right shoulder pain with overhead strokes. The examiner flexes her arm and elbow to 90 degrees and internally rotates the shoulder, causing sharp pain (positive Hawkins test).
oneliner: 38F swimmer, overhead pain + pain on internal rotation of flexed arm → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: Instability causes apprehension on external rotation; she has **pain on internal rotation**
whyNot.B: Biceps tendinopathy hurts on resisted flexion; she has **pain on internal rotation**
whyNot.D: Adhesive capsulitis stiffens all passive motion; hers is **pain on internal rotation**
whyNot.E: AC sprain follows a fall onto the shoulder; she has **overhead swimming pain**

why: Pain on internal rotation of the forward-flexed arm is a positive Hawkins test: the supraspinatus tendon is pinched under the coracoacromial arch. **Overhead activity** causes subacromial impingement.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Arm falls when lowered from 90 degrees
Weak painful elevation with thumbs down
Pain on internal rotation of flexed arm
Fear when arm abducted, externally rotated
Pain on resisted forward flexion, palm up

idea.rule: Pain on internal rotation of the flexed arm = Hawkins test = subacromial impingement.
also: Neer test: pain on passive forward flexion
Painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees

set_title: Shoulder exam tests: Drop arm test, Empty can test, Hawkins test, Apprehension test and Speed test
stem: A 22-year-old rugby player dislocated his right glenohumeral joint 6 months ago. When the examiner abducts and externally rotates the arm to 90 degrees, he becomes anxious and resists further movement, saying it feels like it will pop out (apprehension test).
oneliner: 22M rugby player, prior dislocation + fear on abduction and external rotation → ?

whyNot.B: Posterior instability occurs with flexion and internal rotation; his is **abduction with external rotation**
whyNot.C: Impingement hurts on internal rotation; he is **fearful with abduction and external rotation**
whyNot.D: Cuff tear causes weakness; he has **fear of the joint popping out**
whyNot.E: A clavicle fracture gives point tenderness and deformity; he has **fear of dislocation**

why: Fear of dislocation as the arm is abducted and externally rotated is a positive apprehension test, indicating anterior glenohumeral instability. **Prior dislocation** is the usual setting.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Arm falls when lowered from 90 degrees
Weak painful elevation with thumbs down
Pain on internal rotation of flexed arm
Fear when arm abducted, externally rotated
Pain on resisted forward flexion, palm up

idea.rule: Fear on abduction plus external rotation = apprehension test = anterior shoulder instability.
also: Bankart lesion: anteroinferior labral tear
Axillary nerve injury can accompany dislocation

set_title: Ankle, wrist and spine tests: Thompson test, Finkelstein test, Snuffbox tenderness, FABER (Patrick) test and Schober test
stem: A 42-year-old man felt a pop behind his right ankle while sprinting for a tennis ball and cannot push off. With him prone and the knees flexed, squeezing the right calf causes no foot movement; squeezing the left calf plantarflexes the foot.
oneliner: 42M, pop behind right ankle + calf squeeze causes no plantarflexion → ?

whyNot.B: Finkelstein tests thumb tendons at the wrist; his problem is the **calf and ankle**
whyNot.C: Snuffbox tenderness is a wrist finding; his complaint is **posterior ankle pain**
whyNot.D: FABER stresses the hip and sacroiliac joint; his finding is a **calf squeeze**
whyNot.E: Schober measures lumbar flexion; his finding is a **calf squeeze, no plantarflexion**

why: A calf squeeze that fails to plantarflex the foot is a positive Thompson test. It shows a ruptured Achilles tendon; fluoroquinolones are a classic risk.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Calf squeeze fails to plantarflex foot
Thumb-in-fist ulnar deviation hurts radial wrist
Hip flexed, abducted, externally rotated hurts SI joint
Little lumbar lengthening on forward bend

idea.rule: No plantarflexion on calf squeeze = Achilles tendon rupture (Thompson test).
also: Fluoroquinolones and steroids raise rupture risk
Intact tendon: squeeze plantarflexes the foot

set_title: Ankle, wrist and spine tests: Thompson test, Finkelstein test, Snuffbox tenderness, FABER (Patrick) test and Schober test
stem: A 20-year-old woman falls on her outstretched hand on ice. Her wrist is not swollen, but pressing the hollow between the thumb extensor tendons at the base of the thumb causes sharp pain. The first wrist x-ray looks normal.
oneliner: 20F, fall on outstretched hand + pain in the hollow at thumb base, normal x-ray → ?

whyNot.A: Thompson test is a calf squeeze; she has **thumb-base pain**
whyNot.C: Finkelstein needs thumb-in-fist ulnar deviation; hers is **pressure pain after a fall**
whyNot.D: FABER stresses the hip and sacroiliac joint; her pain is at the **wrist**
whyNot.E: Schober measures lumbar flexion; her pain is at the **thumb base**

why: Tenderness in the anatomic snuffbox after a fall means scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise. Early x-rays can be normal; avascular necrosis is the risk.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Calf squeeze fails to plantarflex foot
Thumb-in-fist ulnar deviation hurts radial wrist
Hip flexed, abducted, externally rotated hurts SI joint
Little lumbar lengthening on forward bend

idea.rule: Snuffbox pain after a fall = scaphoid fracture, even if the x-ray is normal.
also: Retrograde blood supply risks avascular necrosis
Treat with thumb spica splint; repeat imaging

set_title: Ankle, wrist and spine tests: Thompson test, Finkelstein test, Snuffbox tenderness, FABER (Patrick) test and Schober test
stem: A 29-year-old woman, 3 months postpartum, has radial-sided wrist pain that worsens when she lifts her infant. When she tucks her thumb inside a fist and tilts the wrist toward the little finger, pain over the radial styloid becomes sharp (positive Finkelstein test).
oneliner: 29F, postpartum, radial wrist pain + pain on thumb-in-fist ulnar deviation → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

options.E: Osteoarthritis of the first carpometacarpal joint

whyNot.A: Scaphoid fracture gives snuffbox tenderness after a fall; she has **no trauma**
whyNot.B: Carpal tunnel causes median-nerve numbness; her pain is **radial and tendon provoked**
whyNot.C: Trigger finger locks a digit in flexion; she has **radial styloid pain**
whyNot.E: First carpometacarpal arthritis hurts at the thumb base; hers is **radial styloid pain**

why: Pain on ulnar deviation with the thumb tucked in indicates De Quervain tenosynovitis, inflammation of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons; new mothers are often affected.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Calf squeeze fails to plantarflex foot
Thumb-in-fist ulnar deviation hurts radial wrist
Hip flexed, abducted, externally rotated hurts SI joint
Little lumbar lengthening on forward bend

idea.rule: Pain with thumb-in-fist ulnar deviation = De Quervain tenosynovitis.
also: Involves APL and EPB in first compartment
Common in new mothers lifting infants

set_title: Ankle, wrist and spine tests: Thompson test, Finkelstein test, Snuffbox tenderness, FABER (Patrick) test and Schober test
stem: A 24-year-old man has 8 months of low back pain and stiffness that is worst in the morning, lasts over an hour and improves with exercise. On forward bending, a 10-cm line marked above the lumbosacral junction lengthens by only 2 cm (abnormal Schober test).
oneliner: 24M, morning back stiffness improves with exercise + lumbar line lengthens only 2 cm → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: Disc herniation causes radicular pain; he has **stiffness easing with exercise**
whyNot.B: Spinal stenosis affects older adults; he is **24 with stiffness easing on exercise**
whyNot.D: Lumbar osteoarthritis occurs later in life; he is **24, stiffness easing with exercise**
whyNot.E: Muscle strain is acute after lifting; he has **8 months of inflammatory pain**

why: Reduced lumbar flexion with inflammatory back pain at a young age points to ankylosing spondylitis. Sacroiliitis is early; HLA-B27 is the association.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Calf squeeze fails to plantarflex foot
Thumb-in-fist ulnar deviation hurts radial wrist
Hip flexed, abducted, externally rotated hurts SI joint
Little lumbar lengthening on forward bend

idea.rule: Young man, inflammatory back pain, little lumbar flexion = ankylosing spondylitis.
also: HLA-B27 positive; bamboo spine late
Chest expansion is often reduced

set_title: Pediatric hip signs: Ortolani sign, Barlow sign, Galeazzi sign, Trendelenburg sign and Drehmann sign
stem: A 3-week-old girl, firstborn and delivered breech, is examined supine with hips and knees flexed. As the examiner gently abducts the left hip while lifting the greater trochanter, the femoral head moves into the socket with a palpable clunk.
oneliner: 3-week-old breech firstborn girl + clunk as flexed hip abducted → ?

whyNot.A: Barlow dislocates a reduced hip by adduction and push; this hip **reduces on abduction**
whyNot.B: Galeazzi is unequal knee height; here there is a **clunk on abduction**
whyNot.C: Trendelenburg is pelvic drop in stance; she is an **infant with a clunk**
whyNot.D: Drehmann is forced external rotation on flexion; she has a **clunk on abduction**

why: A clunk as the flexed hip is abducted is a positive Ortolani sign: a dislocated femoral head is relocating into the acetabulum in developmental hip dysplasia.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Clunk as dislocated hip reduces on abduction
Hip dislocates with adduction and posterior push
Knees at unequal height, hips flexed
Unilateral hip dislocation or short femur
Pelvis drops opposite the stance leg
Weak hip abductors, superior gluteal nerve
Passive hip flexion forces external rotation

idea.rule: Clunk on abducting a flexed infant hip = Ortolani; dislocated hip reducing.
also: Risks: breech, firstborn, female, oligohydramnios
Screen with ultrasound at 4-6 weeks

set_title: Pediatric hip signs: Ortolani sign, Barlow sign, Galeazzi sign, Trendelenburg sign and Drehmann sign
stem: A 6-month-old girl lies supine with both hips and knees flexed and feet flat on the table. The left knee sits visibly lower than the right. Abduction of the left hip is limited.
oneliner: 6-month-old girl, hips and knees flexed + left knee lower than right → ?

whyNot.A: Ortolani is a palpable clunk on abduction; here the **knees are unequal in height**
whyNot.B: Barlow is a provocative adduction maneuver for a dislocatable hip; here **knee height differs**
whyNot.D: Trendelenburg needs standing and pelvic drop; she is **supine at 6 months**
whyNot.E: Drehmann is an adolescent SCFE sign; she is **6 months old with unequal knees**

why: Knees at unequal height with hips flexed is the Galeazzi sign. It points to unilateral hip dislocation (or a short femur); the dislocated side appears lower.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Clunk as dislocated hip reduces on abduction
Hip dislocates with adduction and posterior push
Knees at unequal height, hips flexed
Unilateral hip dislocation or short femur
Pelvis drops opposite the stance leg
Weak hip abductors, superior gluteal nerve
Passive hip flexion forces external rotation

idea.rule: Unequal knee heights with hips flexed = Galeazzi; unilateral dislocated hip.
also: Also seen with a short femur
Bilateral dislocation can hide the sign

set_title: Pediatric hip signs: Ortolani sign, Barlow sign, Galeazzi sign, Trendelenburg sign and Drehmann sign
stem: A 2-day-old firstborn girl born breech has her hips flexed and adducted by the examiner, who presses the thigh backward. The left femoral head slips out of the acetabulum (positive Barlow sign).
oneliner: 2-day-old breech girl + hip dislocates on adduction and posterior push → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: Slipped epiphysis affects obese adolescents; she is a **2-day-old newborn**
whyNot.B: Perthes is avascular necrosis at ages 4-8; she is a **newborn**
whyNot.C: Septic arthritis causes fever and refusal to move; she has **a provocative-maneuver slip only**
whyNot.E: Transient synovitis follows a viral illness in children; she is a **newborn**

why: A hip that can be dislocated by adduction and posterior pressure is a positive Barlow sign of developmental hip dysplasia. Breech, female and firstborn are risk factors.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Clunk as dislocated hip reduces on abduction
Hip dislocates with adduction and posterior push
Knees at unequal height, hips flexed
Unilateral hip dislocation or short femur
Pelvis drops opposite the stance leg
Weak hip abductors, superior gluteal nerve
Passive hip flexion forces external rotation

idea.rule: Hip dislocates with adduction and push (Barlow) = developmental hip dysplasia.
also: Ortolani relocates; Barlow dislocates
Treat with Pavlik harness

set_title: Pediatric hip signs: Ortolani sign, Barlow sign, Galeazzi sign, Trendelenburg sign and Drehmann sign
stem: A 35-year-old man develops a limp after an intramuscular injection into the upper inner (superomedial) right buttock. When he stands on his right leg, his left pelvis drops (positive Trendelenburg sign).
oneliner: 35M, injection upper inner right buttock + left pelvis drops standing on right leg → ?
ask: Which nerve is most likely injured?

whyNot.A: Inferior gluteal injury weakens hip extension; his problem is **pelvic drop on stance**
whyNot.C: Sciatic injury weakens knee flexion and foot movement; he has **pelvic drop only**
whyNot.D: Obturator injury weakens thigh adduction; he has **abductor weakness**
whyNot.E: Lateral femoral cutaneous injury causes only thigh sensory loss; he has **pelvic drop**

why: The pelvis drops on the side opposite the weak abductors. Gluteus medius and minimus, supplied by the superior gluteal nerve, are weak on the stance side.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Clunk as dislocated hip reduces on abduction
Hip dislocates with adduction and posterior push
Knees at unequal height, hips flexed
Unilateral hip dislocation or short femur
Pelvis drops opposite the stance leg
Weak hip abductors, superior gluteal nerve
Passive hip flexion forces external rotation

idea.rule: Pelvis drops opposite the stance leg = weak abductors, superior gluteal nerve.
also: Gluteus medius and minimus abduct the hip
Safer site: upper outer quadrant

set_title: Nutrition deficiency signs: Bitot spots, Corkscrew hairs, Casal necklace, Rachitic rosary and Flaky paint dermatosis
stem: A 14-month-old dark-skinned girl, exclusively breastfed without supplements, is not yet walking. She has bowed legs, widened wrists and palpable beading along the costochondral junctions. Alkaline phosphatase is high.
oneliner: 14-month-old F, breastfed + bowed legs + wide wrists + rib beading → ?
ask: Which vitamin deficiency best explains these findings?

whyNot.A: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia, not **wrist widening and rib beading**
whyNot.B: Vitamin E deficiency causes hemolysis and ataxia, not **bowed legs with rib beading**
whyNot.D: Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding; she has **bowed legs and widened wrists**
whyNot.E: B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy, not **bowing and wrist widening**

why: Beading at the costochondral junctions with bowed legs and widened wrists is rickets; **exclusive breastfeeding without supplements** leads to vitamin D deficiency.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Peeling patches with edema and big belly

idea.rule: Costochondral beading + bowed legs + wide wrists in infancy = rickets, low vitamin D.
also: Breast milk is low in vitamin D
Craniotabes and frontal bossing also occur

set_title: Bone imaging signs: Codman triangle, Sunburst pattern, Onion skin periosteum, Soap bubble lesion, Punched-out lytic lesions and Hair-on-end skull
stem: A 15-year-old boy has 6 weeks of progressive pain and swelling above the right knee, worse at night. A radiograph of the distal femur shows a destructive metaphyseal lesion; at its edge, the periosteum is lifted off the cortex with a wedge of new bone beneath.
oneliner: 15M, night knee pain + destructive metaphyseal lesion + lifted periosteum at edge → ?

whyNot.A: Sunburst shows radiating spicules; his finding is a **lifted periosteal edge**
whyNot.B: Onion skin is layered diaphyseal bone; his lesion is **metaphyseal with a lifted edge**
whyNot.D: Soap bubble is an expansile epiphyseal lytic lesion; his is **metaphyseal with periosteal lifting**
whyNot.E: Punched-out lesions are round lytic holes, not a **lifted periosteal wedge**

why: Periosteum lifted at the tumor edge with new bone beneath is a Codman triangle, classic for osteosarcoma of the **distal femoral metaphysis**.

idea.rule: Elevated periosteum at a metaphyseal lesion margin = Codman triangle, osteosarcoma.
also: Sunburst pattern is the companion sign
Also seen in Ewing sarcoma, osteomyelitis

set_title: Bone imaging signs: Codman triangle, Sunburst pattern, Onion skin periosteum, Soap bubble lesion, Punched-out lytic lesions and Hair-on-end skull
stem: An 11-year-old boy has 3 weeks of thigh pain, low-grade fever and a warm, tender mass. A radiograph shows a lytic lesion in the mid-femoral shaft with concentric layers of new bone along its surface.
oneliner: 11yo M, thigh pain + low-grade fever + mid-shaft lytic lesion, concentric new bone layers → ?

whyNot.A: Codman triangle is one lifted wedge; his shows **multiple layers on the shaft**
whyNot.B: Sunburst has radiating spicules; his bone shows **concentric layers**
whyNot.C: Soap bubble is expansile and epiphyseal; his lesion is **diaphyseal with layered bone**
whyNot.D: Punched-out lesions lack new bone; his has **concentric new bone layers**

why: **Concentric layers of new bone** around a diaphyseal lytic lesion in a child give the onion skin appearance, classic for Ewing sarcoma t(11;22).

idea.rule: Diaphyseal lytic lesion with layered new bone in a child = Ewing sarcoma.
also: t(11;22) EWS-FLI1 fusion
Small round blue cells on biopsy

set_title: Bone imaging signs: Codman triangle, Sunburst pattern, Onion skin periosteum, Soap bubble lesion, Punched-out lytic lesions and Hair-on-end skull
stem: A 27-year-old woman has 4 months of pain near the left knee. A radiograph shows an eccentric, expansile, multiloculated lytic lesion in the distal femoral epiphysis reaching the subchondral bone, with a thin, well-defined rim.
oneliner: 27F, knee pain + expansile multiloculated lytic epiphyseal lesion → ?
ask: Which diagnosis best explains this finding?

whyNot.B: Osteosarcoma is metaphyseal and sclerotic or spiculated, not **epiphyseal and purely lytic**
whyNot.C: Ewing sarcoma is diaphyseal with layered new bone, not **epiphyseal lysis**
whyNot.D: Osteochondroma is a cartilage-capped outgrowth, not a **lytic epiphyseal lesion**
whyNot.E: Metastasis is unlikely at 27 and rarely **expansile and epiphyseal**

why: An expansile, multiloculated lytic **epiphyseal** lesion in a young adult is the soap bubble appearance of giant cell tumor, with multinucleated giant cells.

idea.rule: Expansile lytic epiphyseal lesion in young adult = giant cell tumor (soap bubble).
also: Biopsy: multinucleated giant cells, stromal cells
Can recur locally; rarely metastasizes

set_title: Vascular bedside tests: Homans sign, Allen test, Adson test, Blue toe syndrome and Arm blood pressure difference
stem: A 31-year-old woman, a competitive swimmer, has numbness of the right ring and little fingers and arm heaviness when working overhead. Her radial pulse fades when she turns her head to the right, extends her neck and inhales deeply.
oneliner: 31F, swimmer + ulnar-side finger numbness + radial pulse fades with neck turn and inhalation → ?
ask: Which condition best explains these findings?

options.C: Pancoast tumor invading the brachial plexus

whyNot.A: Subclavian steal lowers arm pressure at rest; hers fades only with **neck turning**
whyNot.B: Carpal tunnel affects thumb to radial ring finger, not **ring and little fingers**
whyNot.C: Pancoast tumor adds Horner syndrome and shoulder pain; she is a **healthy 31-year-old**
whyNot.D: Takayasu arteritis weakens pulses at rest, not **pulse loss only with neck turning**

why: Radial pulse fading with neck rotation, extension and deep inspiration is a positive Adson test, from neurovascular compression at the thoracic outlet (cervical rib or **scalenes**).

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Palm stays pale after ulnar release
Inadequate ulnar collateral flow (radial puncture unsafe)
Radial pulse fades with neck turn, deep breath
Lower BP and weak pulse in one arm

idea.rule: Pulse loss with neck turn and inspiration = Adson test, thoracic outlet syndrome.
also: Cervical rib or scalene hypertrophy
Lower brachial plexus: ulnar-side paresthesia
